title: The rain on the plants (Kern ch. 5)
hook: one rain falls on all plants, and each grows by its own nature

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disciples saw they had been the Buddha's heirs from the start, working for a wage when the treasure was theirs. Your line: heirs all along. Did you use the inheritance you named? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-eight.

A summer storm doesn't check the garden plan before it rains. The same water lands on the tomatoes, the weeds by the fence, the old maple and the moss between the paving stones. And the next morning, each of them has done something different with it. The tomato swells. The maple pushes out new leaves. The moss turns bright green. The disciples have just told their story of the lost son. In chapter five the Buddha answers them, and he chooses weather. Today: the rain on the plants.
screen: `A STORM WITH NO GARDEN PLAN.` → `SAME WATER, EVERY PLANT.` → `THE BUDDHA ANSWERS WITH WEATHER.`

segments.voice: First, the cloud. In Kern's translation the Buddha tells Kasyapa about a great cloud that rises and spreads over the whole world, covering everything. Then it rains, everywhere at once. Second, the plants. The rain falls on grasses, bushes, herbs and trees, small, middle-sized and large, on every kind of growing thing on mountains, in valleys and on the plains. The rain doesn't choose. It is one rain, the sutra says, of a single taste. But each plant takes up the water according to its own nature and size, and grows, flowers and bears fruit in its own way. A blade of grass doesn't become an oak. It becomes more fully grass. Third, the meaning. The Buddha says he is like that cloud. He appears in the world and teaches gods, humans and all beings alike, and his teaching has one taste: the taste of release. He doesn't hold some people back and pour more on others. He is equal toward everyone, the sutra says, the noble and the poor, those who keep the rules and those who break them, the quick and the slow. The difference is in the receiving. Each one hears the teaching according to their own capacity, and grows from there. Fourth, the link. Notice how this fits the last few days. In chapter two the teaching took many shapes. Here the Buddha says the source of all those shapes is one. The many ways belong to the hearers, like the many plants. The one goal belongs to the rain. The picture makes no demands. It doesn't ask the grass to be a tree. It doesn't ask the tree to apologize for being tall. It just keeps raining, on everyone, and lets each one grow toward the same light in the way only it can.
screen: `A CLOUD OVER THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `ONE RAIN, EACH PLANT ITS OWN WAY.` · `ONE TASTE, EQUAL TO ALL.` · `MANY HEARERS, ONE SOURCE.` · then, large: `ONE RAIN, MANY PLANTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: water one plant. If there's a plant near you, a houseplant, a window box, a tree by the door, give it some water now, slowly, and watch the soil take it in. If there isn't, sit and picture one. Then settle and breathe. Let each in-breath be like rain arriving, and each out-breath like the plant quietly using it. No hurry. Let it take what it can. The bell holds the time.

The rain on the plants. The Buddha's parable in chapter five: one rain of one taste falls on every plant, and each grows by its own nature; one teaching, and each being receives it in their own way. Today's word.
screen: `THE RAIN ON THE PLANTS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: one rain, many plants. Today, give the same kindness to two very different people, and watch what each one does with it. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: The parable of the medicinal plants in chapter five of the Lotus Sutra is taught in East Asian Buddhism as a picture of the Buddha's equal compassion: one teaching, received differently by each person according to their capacity.

fork.setup: you are a small herb under a great tree when the rain comes. what happens to you?
options: the tree takes all the water first
you take up what you can and grow as an herb
you grow into a tree yourself
fork.reveal: the rain falls on all alike, and each plant takes it up by its own nature and size; the herb grows fully as an herb.

original.note: Sanskrit: medicinal plants, herbs; the name of chapter five in Kern's Sanskrit text.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice nature image.
what it means: the Buddha's teaching is one and equal toward all; beings receive it according to their own capacity.
what a scholar hears: chapter five turns chapter two's many ways around: the variety belongs to the hearers, and the teaching itself is of one taste, release.

notes: Chapter 5 paraphrased from Kern (SBE XXI, 1884); nothing quoted.

Check: the Buddha addresses Kasyapa; the cloud covering the world (Kern gives a cosmological scale, omitted); the plants of small, middle and large size; the 'one taste' of the teaching as the taste of deliverance or release; the Buddha's equality toward the noble and the low, the virtuous and the unvirtuous.
Kern's Sanskrit chapter 5 also contains the potter and the blind-man parables, absent from Kumarajiva's Chinese; not taught here. Keeper may want a note on the difference.
Original: oshadhi (ओषधी) as chapter-five title (Oshadhiparivarta); check spelling and stress.

Editor: replaced the uplift line 'there's a gentleness in this picture'; practice line 'nothing to become except more fully what you already are' cut (it told the listener what they are, and sat oddly with the one-vehicle promise).
